opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the most interesting work in RL right now isn't really happening at the level of the training algorithm. It's happening in the environments: the tasks, the rubrics, the tools, the harnesses, all the stuff that defines what you're actually asking the model to get good at. And right now most of that work lives inside the big labs, behind closed doors. Every lab has its own internal pile of environments and evals, and none of it is shared. So if you're a researcher or a small team or just someone who's really good at one domain, there's no real way to contribute to the frontier, or even to build on what other people have done.

GitHub is a nice mental model because it solved that problem for software. Before it you had code scattered everywhere. After it you had a place where you could find something, fork it, improve it, open a PR, and everyone benefits. We want that same dynamic for environments. Someone builds a great environment for, say, legal reasoning or some weird scientific workflow. Someone else forks it, makes the rubric better, adds harder tasks. A third person takes a bunch of those and trains a model on them. It compounds.

The other piece is that it's not just a repository. It's connected to the actual infrastructure for running evals and doing training. So it's not "here's some code, good luck." It's "here's an environment, and with a few commands you can evaluate your model on it or train against it." That closes the loop between people who know what good behavior looks like in a domain and people who have the compute and tooling to actually optimize for it.

Honestly, a big part of it is a bet on openness. I don't think a handful of companies should be the only ones deciding what models get trained to do. If environments are where a lot of the capability comes from, then making environments a community, open-source thing is one of the most leveraged ways to make the whole ecosystem more open. A community platform is how you get the long tail. There are thousands of domains where the real experts aren't at any lab, and we want to give them a place to plug in.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared environments made from tasks, rubrics, tools, and harnesses that people can fork and improve, then use to train models against.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that I keep coming back to is that the hardest part of RL right now isn't the algorithms. It's the environments. Every lab, every startup, every grad student is building their own little harness for the same handful of tasks, and almost none of that work gets shared in a way that someone else can actually pick up and run.

And when I think about what made software go from this artisanal thing to something with real compounding, it's GitHub. Not Git by itself. Git existed for years before GitHub. What GitHub did was make it trivial to find someone else's thing, fork it, change one line, and send that back. The social layer was the unlock, not the version control.

Environments have that same shape. An environment is basically a repo. It has a task definition, a reward function, maybe a sandbox, some data. If I build a good environment for, say, coding agents working on a real codebase, that's useful to a lot of people. But today the way you'd share it is a tweet and a zip file, and nobody builds on it because there's no shared format and no place to put it.

So the dream for Lab is: you have a canonical place where environments live, they all conform to the same interface, you can see who's running them, what models have been evaluated on them, what the leaderboard looks like, and crucially you can fork one and extend it. Somebody takes my math environment and adds a harder tier. Somebody else notices the reward function is exploitable and sends a fix. That feedback loop is what makes a community rather than a directory.

The other piece is that this lowers the bar for who gets to do RL. Right now you kind of need a team and a lot of infra to do anything serious. If the environments are just there and you can plug a model into them in an afternoon, then a single person with a good idea about a task can contribute something real. That's how you get the long tail of weird, specific, valuable environments that no lab would prioritize internally.

And honestly, the incentive structure matters too. On GitHub you get stars, you get a profile, people know what you built. We want that for environments. If you build the environment that ends up being the thing everyone trains on for some capability, you should get credit for that, not have it vanish into some lab's internal eval suite.

r001.rationale: The response describes shareable environments with task definitions, reward functions, and sandboxes that others can plug models into to do RL, including coding-agent tasks. This clearly communicates reusable model-training environments, equivalent to the criterion’s post-training workflows.

astra-6.text: What I like about GitHub is that it makes it easy to build on other people’s work. You can share something, someone else can try it, they can improve it, and those improvements can flow back to everyone else. I want Lab to have that same dynamic—a place where people can share what they’re working on, learn from each other, and collaborate. The community should help make the platform more useful than anything we could build on our own.

r001.rationale: The response describes sharing and improving community work generally, but does not identify models or tools as environments others can use to post-train models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing about GitHub is that it makes it possible for people to build on each other’s work without having to coordinate everything in advance. You can find a project, understand what someone tried, fork it, and contribute something back. I want Lab to make that kind of collaboration possible around training models.

A lot of the useful knowledge is in the process: what environment you used, what you rewarded, what worked, and what failed. If we can make those things easy to share and reproduce, then someone’s experiment becomes a starting point for the next person. The community can accumulate progress instead of everyone having to rediscover the same things independently.

r001.rationale: The response describes sharing and reproducing training experiments so others can build on them, but does not clearly say that shared workflows involving models or tools serve as environments others can use to post-train models.
